en.title: Min Jin Lee: Facing Mortality Inspired 'Pachinko' Author's Literary Journey
en.summary: The acclaimed author of Pachinko, Min Jin Lee, reveals the profound personal health scare that fueled her determination to write. Her powerful words underscore the urgency she felt to create, even when facing life-threatening circumstances.
en.body:
## A Life-Altering Diagnosis Fuels a Literary Fire

When **Min Jin Lee** was in her mid-twenties, a daunting medical diagnosis reshaped her life's trajectory. Told she was a carrier of hepatitis B and highly likely to develop liver cancer, the future author made a powerful vow to herself. "I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first," Lee shared in a recent interview, reflecting on the pivotal moment that led her to abandon a career in corporate law. This stark confrontation with mortality ignited a fierce drive to create, prioritizing her literary ambitions above financial security and conventional healthcare. The weight of her prognosis meant she felt a constant, underlying urgency to leave her mark through storytelling.

Now 57 and looking remarkably healthy, Lee, the Korean-American author behind the international bestseller **Pachinko** and **Free Food for Millionaires**, is preparing to release her third novel, **American Hagwon**. This new book completes what she initially termed her "Korean trilogy," though she playfully corrected an interviewer, calling it a "Korean quartet." Thanks to advancements in experimental medicine, Lee is in good health and is already planning her next manuscript, aiming to complete it before she turns 70. "I’m writing the four books that I wanted to write and after that I’m going to take a long nap," she quipped, showcasing her characteristic blend of gravitas and humor.

## The Enduring Power of **Pachinko** and its Legacy

**Pachinko**, published in 2017, resonated deeply with readers worldwide, selling millions of copies and leading to a critically acclaimed Apple TV+ adaptation in 2022. The novel's epic scope, tracing the lives of a Korean immigrant family across generations, struck a chord with its exploration of identity, belonging, and resilience. Lee's ability to weave intricate narratives that are both deeply personal and universally relatable has cemented her status as a vital voice in contemporary literature. For fans, her journey from a precarious health outlook to becoming a celebrated author is a testament to the power of perseverance and the profound impact of storytelling.

## What's Next for Min Jin Lee

With **American Hagwon** on the horizon, readers anticipate the continuation of Lee's exploration of Korean identity and history. While specific release details for **American Hagwon** are still emerging, her dedication to completing her ambitious literary project signals more compelling narratives to come from this masterful storyteller.

content_raw: Her last novel sold 5m copies and was adapted into a hit series. Nearly 10 years on, the Korean-American author has written another epic. She discusses ambition and the diagnosis that inspired her to leave work and write Back in 1995, when she was in her mid-20s, Min Jin Lee quit her job as a corporate lawyer. As a teenager she had been diagnosed as a hepatitis B carrier and doctors told her she was highly likely to develop liver cancer in her 20s or 30s. “I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first,” the now 57-year-old Korean-American author says of her decision to turn her back on a regular pay cheque and healthcare. “I was told so many times that I was going to get sicker and sicker, that I’ve always felt that if I can get a really good book out then I’m done.” Lee, looking very much alive and well, is on a video call from her home in Harlem, New York, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves behind her. We are meeting to discuss the publication of her third novel, American Hagwon, the final part in what she calls her “Korean trilogy”, following Free Food for Millionaires in 2007 and her 2017 international bestseller, Pachinko , stylishly adapted for Apple TV in 2022. “Korean quartet!” she corrects me now. Thanks to experimental drugs, she is now so healthy she can commit to another book. “Before I turn 70, I should turn in my manuscript,” she jokes. “I’m writing the four books that I wanted to write and after that I’m going to take a long nap.” Continue reading...
